## Who Is This Actually For?

When you're designing something — an app, a website, a tool, a document — there's always a person on the other end who has to use it. That person has goals, abilities, and expectations that shape what "good" looks like.

If your prompt doesn't mention that person, the AI will fill in the blank with assumptions. Often those assumptions are a generic adult user with average technical skills, a lot of time, and no particular needs. That might not match your actual user at all.

Adding user context means telling the AI who the end user is, so it can tailor its output to actually fit them.

## When and Why to Name a User

You don't need user context for every prompt. But it matters whenever the output is going to be experienced or used by someone other than you — or when the *audience* meaningfully affects what a good response looks like.

Ask yourself: *Who has to actually use, read, or interact with what I'm building?*

If the answer is someone specific — a younger student, a first-time app user, a teacher who isn't technical, a person with accessibility needs — name them. That context changes what the AI produces.

## How User Context Changes AI Output

Here's the same task prompted two different ways:

**Without user context:**
> "Write error messages for my app when a user enters an incorrect password."

The AI might write something like:
> *"Error 401: Authentication failed. Invalid credentials."*

Technically accurate — but confusing to most real users. What does "Error 401" mean to a middle schooler? What should they actually *do* next?

**With user context:**
> "Write error messages for my app when a user enters an incorrect password. The users are middle school students who may not be familiar with technical terms. The message should be friendly, clearly explain what went wrong, and tell them exactly what to do next."

Now the AI might write:
> *"That password doesn't match what we have on file. Double-check for typos and try again — remember, passwords are case-sensitive!"*

Same task. Completely different result. The user context is what changed it.

## More Side-by-Side Examples

**Explaining a concept**

> ❌ "Explain how the electoral college works."

> ✅ "Explain how the electoral college works for a group of 9th graders who just started learning about how elections work. Avoid assuming they know any political vocabulary. Use a simple analogy to make it concrete, and keep it to a few short paragraphs."

**Writing instructions**

> ❌ "Write instructions for how to submit an assignment on our class website."

> ✅ "Write step-by-step instructions for how to submit an assignment on our class website. The audience is students who've never used the site before and may be nervous about doing it wrong. Use plain language, number each step clearly, and include a note about what to do if something doesn't look right."

**A written summary**

> ❌ "Summarize this article about renewable energy."

> ✅ "Summarize this article about renewable energy for a 10th grade class that just started learning about climate science. Keep it under 150 words, avoid technical jargon, and end with one question that could spark a class discussion."

**App error messages**

> ❌ "Write error messages for my app when a file upload fails."

> ✅ "Write error messages for my app when a file upload fails. The users are high school students who aren't very technical. The message should explain what went wrong in plain language and tell them exactly what to try next — not just that an error occurred."

## What to Include

You don't need a full user profile — just enough detail to shape the output. Ask yourself what's most relevant about this user for this specific task:

- **Who they are:** age, background, role (student, teacher, parent, first-time user)
- **What they're trying to do:** their goal in this moment, not just "use the app"
- **What they might struggle with:** technical language, small text, too many steps, missing context
- **What they shouldn't have to deal with:** jargon, unnecessary complexity, assumptions that don't fit them
- **How much time or attention they have:** someone checking an app between classes has different needs than someone sitting down at a computer with 30 minutes

## What Happens Without It

When you don't include a user, the AI defaults. It picks an audience — usually someone who is patient, comfortable with the subject matter, and not in a rush. That's fine for some situations. But if your actual reader is a nervous freshman, a non-technical parent, or someone encountering this topic for the first time, the default will miss the mark.

The AI isn't wrong to make that assumption — it just doesn't know better. You do. Tell it.

## A Design Mindset, Embedded Early

Adding user context isn't just a prompt trick — it's a habit of thinking about the people who will interact with what you create. That mindset shows up in every part of design: what you build, how you name things, how you explain features, and what you leave out.

When you name the user in your prompt, you're making a design decision. You're saying: *this output should work for a real person, not just look correct to me.*

That's the difference between something that technically works and something that's actually useful.
